title: LandedTheJob
oneLine: An LLM pipeline that turns messy inputs (PDF resumes, scraped job pages) into structured data, then generates job-specific resumes under truthfulness and style constraints.

specs.Role: Sole developer. Built with heavy AI pair-programming (Claude Code), and the commit history shows that.
specs.Built: First working version shipped in two days, 16 to 17 April 2026
specs.Stack: Next.js 15 (App Router, React 19), TypeScript, Prisma 6 on Postgres (Neon), Clerk auth, Stripe billing, Tailwind
specs.Tests: No automated tests or evaluation harness yet

intake.question: What is it, in one sentence?
intake.hint: Fix my sentence if it undersells it.
intake.draft: Paste a job listing and get back a resume rewritten to mirror its language, plus a cover letter pitched at that company's tone. Your own line in the README is better than anything I would write: your resume, rewritten to win.

intake.question: Role, timeline, status
intake.hint: The deployment and users question. Answer it plainly, whichever way it goes.
intake.draft: From the repo: 10 commits across 16 and 17 April 2026, so two days. 59 TypeScript files, 10 Prisma models. The site previously said 58 files and 11 models, both slightly off, and I have corrected them to what the repo counts today. All 10 commits carry a Claude co-author trailer. NEEDS YOU: signups, revenue, generation time per resume, and Anthropic spend per resume. Any one of those beats a file count as the headline. LINEAGE, and it is worth a line on the page: resume-maker, 4 commits in September 2025, is this idea built plain. Express, jsPDF and html2canvas, no framework, and by 30 September it had grown a cover letter maker and a job optimiser. LandedTheJob is the same idea rebuilt seven months later on Next.js, Prisma, Clerk and Stripe with an LLM doing the rewriting. Building a thing, living with it, and rebuilding it properly is a better argument than either version alone. Both repos are public, so the comparison is one a reader can actually make.

intake.question: What made it hard?
intake.hint: Pick one of the three, or tell me I missed it.
intake.draft: Candidates from your own code: LLM-based parsing of job listings pasted in any format (src/lib/parseJobListing.ts and parseJobText.ts), the credits and daily-cap billing model, or the user identity problem you fixed twice. That second one is the best story: you have a commit fixing a race in requireUser with an upsert, and another reclaiming a user row by email when the Clerk ID did not match. That is a real distributed-identity bug and most people never hit it.

intake.question: What did you decide, and what did you reject?
intake.hint: Why the billing model changed on day two.
intake.draft: Straight from your commit log: you switched from a plain subscription to a Pack plus Pro model with a daily cap, one day into the build. That is a genuine product decision with the rejected alternative built right into it. Why? Anthropic cost control? Also worth naming: Clerk over NextAuth, Neon over Supabase, and templates as reference HTML instead of a PDF library.

intake.question: What number can you put on it?
intake.hint: Anything real, even ten users and eleven dollars.
intake.draft: From the repo: 58 TypeScript files, 11 data models, 3 price points ($9/mo, $19/mo, $29 one-time), 10 commits, 2 days. NEEDS YOU: signups, revenue, generation time per resume, Anthropic spend per resume.

intake.question: What broke, and what did you do?
intake.hint: The Clerk ID mismatch, from the user's side.
intake.draft: Three fix commits in the history, and two are the same class of bug, which is the honest shape of an auth story. requireUser hit a race and needed an upsert. Then a user row could not be found when the Clerk id did not match, so it had to be reclaimed by email. The third was the Stripe client initialising at module load and breaking the build, fixed by making it lazy. NEEDS YOU: did the Clerk id mismatch show up as real users locked out of their own accounts? If so, say that, because the consequence is what makes it a story.

intake.question: What media do you have?
intake.hint: Live URL, public repo, screen recording.
intake.draft: In the repo: templates/ holds reference HTML for the resume and cover letter, and docs-spec.md. NEEDS YOU: a live URL, whether the GitHub repo is public, and a screen recording of paste-to-resume. For this project the recording matters more than any screenshot.

intake.question: What would you do differently?
intake.hint: Two sentences. Not self criticism, a design judgment you would make differently now.

intro: LandedTheJob is a deployed web app. It takes a job seeker's career history and a job posting, and produces a resume and cover letter rewritten for that posting.

The resume above is real output from the pipeline, for a made-up candidate and a made-up job posting. It also breaks my own no-fabrication rule. I ran the pipeline once to see what it did, and that run is the center of this page.
This is prompt design, structured extraction, multimodal input handling and output constraint around a hosted model. I did not train or fine-tune anything.

sections.label: Pipeline
sections.title: How it works
body: The app has five separate model call sites. Two turn messy input into structured data. Two generate documents from that data. One rewrites a single bullet.

The model emits JSON and code emits the document. Resume tailoring returns a ResumeData object against a fixed schema. A hand-written renderer escapes every string and places it into a fixed template. The model never writes HTML. That keeps the layout identical across generations, and it means text in a job posting, which is untrusted input, cannot inject markup or change the document structure.

flow.summary: A resume file goes through a profile extraction call into a structured profile in Postgres. A job URL or pasted text is stripped to plain text and goes through a job parsing call into a structured Job row. The profile and the job then feed a resume tailoring call, which returns ResumeData JSON, and a cover letter call, which returns plain text. Both outputs go to a deterministic renderer. A fifth call rewrites a single bullet on request.

sections.label: Inputs
sections.title: Messy inputs, one schema
body: Resume import is routed by file type. PDFs go to the model as native document blocks. Images go through vision. DOCX is converted to text first with mammoth. Everything else is sent as text. One extraction prompt and one schema serve all four paths. The merge into the database is additive: it only fills blank personal fields and dedupes skills case-insensitively, so a bad extraction cannot overwrite what the user typed.

The first job importer parsed JSON-LD and OpenGraph tags. It broke on entity-encoded company names and on sites without structured data. I replaced it with LLM extraction. Now the URL path and the paste path both strip HTML to text and send it through the same extraction prompt and schema, so there is one code path to maintain. Text from a fetched page is cut at 60,000 characters. Pages that return under 100 characters of text are rejected with a message telling the user to paste the listing instead.

sections.label: Constraints
sections.title: Constraining the model
body: The resume prompt carries four sets of rules. Truthfulness: never invent employers, dates, tools or credentials, and omit a required skill rather than claim it. Keyword fidelity: reuse the posting's exact noun phrases, such as "Kubernetes" and not "k8s", where the candidate has the experience. Seniority: match the posting's verb tier, but never over-level. Voice: a banned-word list, no em dashes, varied bullet length and opening verbs. The cover letter prompt adds banned stock openings and asks for uneven sentence lengths.

Where a rule is cheap to check in code, I check it in code. The punctuation rules are enforced after generation by a regex scrub. The template is a single column with plain-text separators, neutral class names and standard section headings, because multi-column grids and styled separators parse badly in applicant tracking systems.
These two excerpts are the rules that the run below broke.

code.text:
Truthfulness rules (non-negotiable):
- Never fabricate experience, employers, dates, tools, or credentials.
- Reuse the candidate's real role titles, companies, and dates exactly.
- If the JD requires a skill the candidate does NOT have in their profile, do not claim it. Omit rather than invent.

[...]

- Match your bullet verbs to the JD's tier, but ONLY when the candidate's actual experience supports that level. Never over-level: if the source material says "helped build", do not write "led the architecture of". When in doubt, stay one tier below the JD rather than inflate.

sections.label: Measured
sections.title: What I measured, and what failed
body: I ran the production pipeline once. The candidate is fictional: "Jordan Rivera", a backend engineer. The posting is fictional too: an ML platform role that requires Kubernetes, Kafka and PyTorch. None of the three appear in the candidate's profile. The employers and the company in the posting are also made up.

The resume output broke the truthfulness rules in three ways. The prompt says to omit a skill the candidate lacks. The model hedged with "(familiar)" instead. It also turned "helped maintain" into "owned" and invented deploy gates. And it added "improving model quality", a phrase lifted from the posting, to a bullet about catching outages.
This is one run. It shows the failure exists. It does not give a rate, and I have not measured how often it happens.
sections.callout: Prompt instructions are a request, not an enforcement mechanism, and the pressure to match a job description pulls directly against a no-fabrication rule.

after: Some things worked in the same run. Job parsing separated the description from the requirements, kept salary and location, and dropped the nav, "Apply now" and recruiter-contact boilerplate. The resume reused the posting's phrasing where the candidate had real backing: "p95 latency", "Amazon Web Services (AWS)", "message queue", "data pipeline". Neither document contained a banned word or an em dash.
The cover letter stated the gap honestly: "I haven't yet worked inside a PyTorch training cluster or written drift detection from scratch."
The full inputs and outputs of the run are in the repo, at docs/portfolio/sample-output/pipeline-run.json.

sections.label: Next
sections.title: What I would build next
body: None of this is built. There are no automated tests and no evaluation harness yet. These are the four pieces I would add, in this order.

cards.title: Grounding check
cards.body: A deterministic check. Every tool or skill term in the output must trace to a term in the stored profile. Otherwise it is removed, or the generation is retried.

cards.title: Evaluation set
cards.body: A small set of profile and posting pairs with deliberate skill gaps, scored for fabricated terms and for posting-keyword coverage. Then prompt changes can be compared by number instead of by reading.

cards.title: Keyword match and gap report
cards.body: Structured keyword extraction from the posting, with a match score and a gap report shown to the user.

cards.title: Structured output
cards.body: Move from parsing JSON out of text to the API's structured output support, so schema violations cannot occur.

sections.label: Around the model
sections.title: Engineering around the model
body: Credits are spent with an atomic conditional update, so two concurrent requests cannot overspend. A failed model call refunds the credit. The Stripe webhook is the single writer of billing state.

Per-user rate limits sit on every model route: 10 resume generations per minute, 5 profile imports per hour, 30 bullet rewrites per minute. The rate limiter is in-memory, which is a known single-instance limitation.
The company context for cover letters is a single fetched page truncated to 6,000 characters. It is not retrieval.

sections.label: Product
sections.title: The live product
body: The app is live at landedthejob.com and the repo is public. I have no user, signup or revenue numbers to report, so I state none.

I am Atreyu Sutton. I am studying for an M.S. in Engineering at the ATLAS Institute, CU Boulder, after a B.A. in Computer Science at Rollins College, and I am looking for AI/ML engineering internships.
